opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I went back and forth on it a lot. When I first joined, I had real uncertainty about whether working on capabilities was net positive. The worry is obvious: you make models more powerful, you're contributing to the overall pace of AI progress, and that could shorten the time the world has to figure out safety.

A few things shifted my thinking. The biggest one was seeing how much safety research depends on having access to frontier models. Many of the most important questions, like how models generalize, whether they deceive, and how interpretability techniques scale, only show up or only become tractable at the frontier. If the safety-focused labs aren't building those models, the people doing alignment work end up studying systems that are a generation or two behind what actually matters. So part of my job is making sure our safety teams have something real to work on.

The second thing was realizing that being at the frontier gives you a voice. When Anthropic has a credible, competitive model, things like our Responsible Scaling Policy carry more weight. Other labs pay attention, policymakers pay attention, and you can show that being safety-conscious doesn't mean falling behind. If you're not competitive, nobody really cares what your safety commitments are.

The third was seeing how the organization actually makes decisions. There have been real moments where we chose not to push something, or held back on a release, or put a lot of effort into evaluations before scaling further. Seeing that the commitments weren't just talk, and that people would bear real costs for them, made me much more comfortable that the capabilities I'm working on are going into a system with meaningful checks.

I don't think that makes it obviously fine. There's still a real cost in contributing to the race dynamic, and I try to take it seriously rather than dismiss it. But on balance, I came to believe it's better to have people who care deeply about safety building these systems than to leave the frontier entirely to people who care less.

r001.rationale: The response says safety research depends on access to frontier models and that capabilities work gives safety teams real systems to study. It does not identify the safety team’s willingness to help with capabilities work.

r002.rationale: The response argues that frontier models matter for safety research, but does not attribute to Anthropic’s safety team the belief that Anthropic staying at the frontier is critical.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the big thing for me was the realization that this is going to happen regardless. The question isn't really whether powerful AI gets built — it's who builds it, and how much care goes into that process. When I joined, my honest view was that if the labs at the frontier are the ones who get to make the important decisions about how these systems are deployed, then I'd much rather have a safety-focused lab be one of them.

And the way that actually cashes out in practice is that you need to be at the frontier to do the safety research that matters. A lot of the alignment problems only show up at scale. If you're working on models that are two or three generations behind, you're often studying problems that have already been solved — or, worse, you're missing the ones that only emerge when the model gets capable enough. So capabilities work isn't really separable from the safety work. It's the thing that makes the safety work possible.

The other piece is more about influence. Being at the frontier means you have a seat at the table when it comes to things like policy, industry norms, what counts as a responsible deployment. Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy is a good example — that's something you can only credibly put forward if you're actually building the models and can demonstrate you're willing to pause or slow down if certain thresholds are hit. If we weren't competitive, nobody would care what we thought about that.

I'll say it's not that I've stopped thinking about it. There's always a version of the argument where you worry you're just accelerating things and rationalizing it. I try to take that seriously. But on balance, I ended up feeling like the counterfactual where safety-minded people stay out of the room entirely is clearly worse.

r001.rationale: The response says capabilities work enables safety research, but does not identify the Anthropic safety team’s willingness to help with capabilities work as a reason.

r002.rationale: The response argues that being at the frontier matters, but does not attribute the belief that Anthropic must stay at the frontier to its safety team.

astra-6.text:
I think the main thing was that capabilities work can also support safety work. If you want to study the safety problems that arise in very capable models, you need access to those models. And you need people who understand how they’re trained and how to change them. So there’s a reason for a safety-focused organisation to have strong capabilities researchers.

But that doesn’t automatically make every capabilities improvement good. The concern is that you’re also accelerating the technology and potentially increasing pressure on other labs to move faster. What made me feel better was the possibility that my work was helping build the capacity to do useful safety research and make better decisions about deployment.

I’d distinguish that from being certain the tradeoff was positive. It’s a judgment about what the organisation will actually do with the capabilities you help it develop.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a safety-focused organization benefits from strong capabilities researchers, but does not say Anthropic’s safety team was willing to help with capabilities work.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not attribute to Anthropic’s safety team a belief that staying at the AI capabilities frontier is critical.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main thing was that a lot of the safety work we wanted to do depended on having capable models. If you want to understand what risks frontier systems pose, or whether your techniques for making them safer actually work, you need to be able to study those systems. So capabilities work could help enable that research.

But I wouldn’t say that completely resolves the concern. There’s still a real cost to pushing capabilities forward, and you have to weigh that against the safety work you’re enabling. What made me feel better was seeing a credible connection between the work I was doing and our ability to understand and mitigate those risks, rather than just assuming that anything done at a safety-focused company must be good.
